wikipedia: The article gives the northern kingdom’s lands, capitals, and fall to Assyria about 720 BCE.
The article gives Judah’s place, capital, and ruling family. It also reports the debate about its early size.
The article reports the debate about the kingdom of Saul, David, and Solomon. Scholars disagree on whether it existed and how large it was.
The article gives the place, neighbors, and end date of the kingdom centered on Damascus.
The article names the five Philistine cities and their coast land. It dates Babylon’s conquest to 604 BCE.
The article describes the Phoenician coast cities, their separate rule, and their sea trade.
The article places Moab east of the Dead Sea. It names Dibon and the stone of King Mesha.
The article places Edom and follows its people’s later move into southern Judah.
The article places Ammon east of the Jordan and names Rabbah as its chief city.
The article places Midian in northwest Arabia. It reports the view that the name first meant a league of tribes.
The article describes Canaan as a region of the southern Levant with many peoples.
The article follows Assyria’s growth from the Tigris to rule over the Levant and Egypt.
The article dates Babylon’s empire from 626 to 539 BCE. It reports the fall of Assyria.
The article gives the Persian Empire’s founding, its reach, and its end under Alexander.
The article describes the Persian province around Jerusalem and names the provinces beside it.
The article says Samaria stayed a seat of government under Assyria, Babylon, and Persia.
The article sums up the Bible’s account of the tribes. It reports that some scholars doubt the twelve-tribe picture.
The article places Bashan in northern Transjordan and reports the Bible’s account of King Og.
The article describes Paddan Aram as the northern plain of Aram Naharaim.
The article dates Herod the Great’s rule and lists the regions of his kingdom.
The article tells how Herod’s kingdom was divided. It dates when each part came under direct Roman rule.
The article dates the Roman province of Judaea and names Caesarea as the governor’s seat.
The article places Perea east of the Jordan, across from Judea and Samaria.
The article lists the ten cities and describes their self-rule under Rome.
The article dates the Roman province of Syria. It reports that Syria later took Philip’s lands.
The article places the province in western Asia Minor and says a proconsul governed it.
The article dates the province to 25 BCE and names Ancyra as its capital.
The article says Pamphylia belonged to Galatia before a later emperor joined it to Lycia.
The article dates the province. It says the Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
The article lists the parts of southern Greece in the province. It says Augustus separated it from Macedonia.
The article dates Roman rule of Cyprus and names Paphos as its capital.
The article places Cilicia on the south coast of Asia Minor. It dates Roman rule from 64 BCE.
The article tells how Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one Black Sea province.
The article dates the province to 17 CE and names Caesarea as its capital.
The article says Rome governed Crete and Cyrenaica as one province.
The article says Italy kept a special status and was not governed like the provinces.
The article gives the road’s course from the Adriatic Sea to Byzantium. It places Paul’s trip from Philippi to Thessalonica on it.
The article lists the road’s stops from Rome to Capua and on to Brundisium. The stops include the Three Taverns and the Market of Appius.
The article gives the road’s course from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. It names a branch to Iconium and Lystra. It dates the road to 6 BCE.
The article describes the pass north of Tarsus. Armies and traders used it for a long time.
The article describes the Persian road from Susa to Sardis and its messenger stations.
The article follows the coast road from Egypt to Damascus. It lists “Way of the Philistines” among the road’s names.
The article follows the trade road across Transjordan to Damascus. It names Edom, Moab, and Ammon among the states that used it.

sources.title: The History of Herodotus, Book 5, chapters 52–54
sources.author: Herodotus; translated by G. C. Macaulay
sources.summary: Herodotus describes the royal road from Sardis to Susa. He counts 111 stations and names the lands and rivers on the way.
sources.limits: Herodotus wrote as a Greek from the west of the empire. He names lands and rivers, not towns. Only chapters 52–54 were read.

land-egypt.name: Egypt · approximate
land-egypt.summary: Egypt lay along the Nile River. Pharaoh ruled it.
land-egypt.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The text does not date these events to a named Pharaoh.

land-canaan.name: Land of Canaan · approximate
land-canaan.summary: Canaan is the Bible’s name for the land west of the Jordan. Many peoples and towns shared it.
land-canaan.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Canaan had no single ruler or fixed border.

land-paddan-aram.name: Paddan Aram · approximate
land-paddan-aram.summary: Paddan Aram is the plain around Haran in upper Mesopotamia.
land-paddan-aram.uncertainty: The shape marks the plain around Haran. The text gives no borders.

midian.name: Midian · approximate
midian.summary: Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba in northwest Arabia. Scholars think the name first meant a league of tribes.
midian.uncertainty: The shape marks a home region. Midianite herders and raiders moved far outside it.

amorite-sihon.name: Sihon’s kingdom · as Numbers describes it
amorite-sihon.summary: Numbers 21 says Sihon, an Amorite king, ruled from the Arnon to the Jabbok. Heshbon was his city.
amorite-sihon.uncertainty: The shape follows the two rivers that Numbers 21:24 names. No other record marks this kingdom.

bashan-og.name: Og’s kingdom in Bashan · as Numbers describes it
bashan-og.summary: Bashan is the high land east of the Sea of Galilee. Numbers 21 names Og as its king.
bashan-og.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to Bashan. The text gives no exact border.

edom.name: Edom · approximate
edom.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
edom.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

moab.name: Moab · approximate
moab.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
moab.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

ammon.name: Ammon · approximate
ammon.summary: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan. Its chief city was Rabbah, now Amman.
ammon.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

israel-tribes.name: Tribes of Israel · approximate
israel-tribes.summary: Israel’s tribes held hill country on both sides of the Jordan. No king ruled them all before Saul.
israel-tribes.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Judges 1 lists towns the tribes did not take. Some scholars doubt the twelve-tribe picture.

israel-united.name: Israel under David and Solomon · approximate
israel-united.summary: The Bible says Saul, David, and Solomon ruled all the tribes as one kingdom. Scholars disagree on how large it was.
israel-united.uncertainty: The shape covers the tribal lands from Dan to Beersheba. It leaves out lands that paid tribute.

israel-north.name: Kingdom of Israel · approximate
israel-north.summary: Ten tribes followed Jeroboam and formed a northern kingdom. Samaria became its capital under Omri.
israel-north.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Its borders with Aram, Moab, and Judah moved often.

judah.name: Kingdom of Judah · approximate
judah.summary: Judah was the southern kingdom. David’s family ruled it from Jerusalem for about four centuries.
judah.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It is not a border for one year.

aram.name: Aram of Damascus · approximate
aram.summary: Aram was a kingdom centered on Damascus. Assyria ended it in 732 BCE.
aram.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Aram and Israel traded control of Gilead and Bashan.

phoenicia.name: Phoenician cities · approximate
phoenicia.summary: Tyre, Sidon, and other coast cities each had their own king. They lived by ships and trade.
phoenicia.uncertainty: The shape joins separate cities along one coast. They were never one kingdom.

philistia.name: Philistine cities · approximate
philistia.summary: Five Philistine cities held the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath.
philistia.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Each city had its own ruler.

egypt.name: Egypt · approximate
egypt.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
egypt.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

assyria-heartland.name: Assyria · home region
assyria-heartland.summary: Assyria’s home lay on the upper Tigris around Assur, Kalhu, and Nineveh. From 745 BCE its kings pushed hard to the west.
assyria-heartland.uncertainty: The shape shows only the home region. Assyria’s reach to the west grew and shrank.

assyria-empire.name: Lands under Assyria · approximate
assyria-empire.summary: Assyria ruled from the Tigris to the Mediterranean through governors and client kings. Its empire fell between 612 and 609 BCE.
assyria-empire.uncertainty: Assyria did not rule all these lands in the same way. The shape is not a border for one year.

babylon-empire.name: Lands under Babylon · approximate
babylon-empire.summary: Babylon replaced Assyria as the great power. Its empire lasted from 626 to 539 BCE.
babylon-empire.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It is not a border for one year.

persia-empire.name: Persian Empire · part shown
persia-empire.summary: Cyrus founded the Persian Empire in 550 BCE and took Babylon in 539 BCE. It reached from Egypt and Asia Minor to the Indus Valley.
persia-empire.uncertainty: The shape shows only the western part of the empire. Its eastern lands lie off this map.

yehud.name: Yehud · Persian province of Judah
yehud.summary: Yehud was the Persian province around Jerusalem. It ran from the western foothills to the Dead Sea.
yehud.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Jerusalem.

samaria-province.name: Samaria · Persian province
samaria-province.summary: Samaria stayed a seat of government under Assyria, Babylon, and Persia.
samaria-province.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province north of Yehud.

herod-kingdom.name: Herod’s kingdom · approximate
herod-kingdom.summary: Herod the Great ruled as king under Rome from 37 to 4 BCE. His kingdom held Judea, Samaria, Galilee, and lands east of the Jordan.
herod-kingdom.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the regions the article lists.

judea-province.name: Judea · Roman province
judea-province.summary: Rome removed Herod’s son Archelaus in 6 CE and made Judea a province. Its governor lived at Caesarea on the coast.
judea-province.uncertainty: The shape joins Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. The province grew after 44 CE.

galilee-antipas.name: Galilee · under Herod Antipas
galilee-antipas.summary: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea until 39 CE.
galilee-antipas.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to Galilee.

perea-antipas.name: Perea · under Herod Antipas
perea-antipas.summary: Perea lay east of the Jordan, across from Judea and Samaria. Herod Antipas ruled it with Galilee.
perea-antipas.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The Gospels do not use the name Perea.

philip-tetrarchy.name: Philip’s lands · approximate
philip-tetrarchy.summary: Philip, another son of Herod, ruled lands northeast of the Jordan until 34 CE.
philip-tetrarchy.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Syria took these lands after Philip died.

decapolis.name: Decapolis · approximate
decapolis.summary: The Decapolis was a group of ten Greek-style cities, most east of the Jordan. Each ran itself under Rome.
decapolis.uncertainty: The shape covers the southern cities only. Some scholars doubt the cities formed one league.

roman-syria.name: Syria · Roman province
roman-syria.summary: Rome made Syria a province in 64 BCE. It bordered the lands of Herod’s family on the north.
roman-syria.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

cilicia.name: Cilicia · approximate
cilicia.summary: Cilicia lay on the south coast of Asia Minor. Rome took it in 64 BCE.
cilicia.uncertainty: The shape shows the eastern plain around Tarsus only.

cyprus.name: Cyprus · Roman province
cyprus.summary: Cyprus was a Roman province under a proconsul. Paphos was its capital.
cyprus.uncertainty: The shape follows the modern coast of the island.

galatia.name: Galatia · Roman province
galatia.summary: Augustus made Galatia a province in 25 BCE. Ancyra was its capital.
galatia.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Pamphylia on the south coast belonged to Galatia for a time.

asia.name: Asia · Roman province
asia.summary: Asia was a rich Roman province in western Asia Minor. A proconsul governed it.
asia.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the province.

bithynia-pontus.name: Bithynia and Pontus · Roman province
bithynia-pontus.summary: Rome joined Bithynia and Pontus into one province on the Black Sea coast.
bithynia-pontus.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the coast lands.

cappadocia.name: Cappadocia · Roman province
cappadocia.summary: Cappadocia became a Roman province in 17 CE. Its capital was a city named Caesarea.
cappadocia.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. This Caesarea is not the port in Judea.

macedonia.name: Macedonia · Roman province
macedonia.summary: Rome made Macedonia a province in 146 BCE. The Via Egnatia crossed it from west to east.
macedonia.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It includes Thessaly and Epirus, which the province held.

achaia.name: Achaia · Roman province
achaia.summary: Achaia covered southern Greece. Augustus made it a province apart from Macedonia.
achaia.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. The province’s islands are not marked.

crete.name: Crete · part of a Roman province
crete.summary: Rome governed Crete together with Cyrenaica in North Africa.
crete.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the island. Cyrenaica is not marked.

italy.name: Italy
italy.summary: Italy was the home region of Rome. It had a special status among Roman lands.
italy.uncertainty: The shape is a simple outline of the peninsula.

genesis.land-egypt: Joseph is sold into Egypt and rises to rule under Pharaoh. Jacob’s family moves there in the famine.
genesis.land-canaan: God promises this land to Abraham’s children. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live in it as outsiders.
genesis.land-paddan-aram: Abraham’s family settles at Haran. Isaac and Jacob both take wives from the family there.
genesis.edom: Esau settles in the hill country of Seir. Genesis 36 lists the chiefs and kings of Edom.

wilderness.land-egypt: Pharaoh enslaves Israel in Egypt. Israel leaves, and the later laws keep recalling that slavery.
wilderness.midian: Moses flees to Midian and marries a priest’s daughter there. Midian’s elders join Moab against Israel in Numbers 22.
wilderness.land-canaan: God promises to bring Israel into Canaan (Exodus 3:8). Twelve spies enter it in Numbers 13.
wilderness.edom: Edom’s king refuses to let Israel pass on the king’s highway (Numbers 20). Israel turns and goes around.
wilderness.moab: Balak king of Moab hires Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 22–24). Moses speaks Deuteronomy in the plains of Moab.
wilderness.ammon: Deuteronomy 2:19 tells Israel not to take Ammon’s land. The text gives it to the children of Lot.
wilderness.amorite-sihon: Sihon refuses to let Israel pass and attacks. Israel defeats him and settles in his towns.
wilderness.bashan-og: Og meets Israel at Edrei and is defeated (Numbers 21:33–35). Half of Manasseh later receives Bashan.

early.israel-tribes: Joshua divides the land by tribe. In Judges each tribe faces its own enemies, and Saul first draws them together.
early.philistia: Samson fights the Philistines, and they capture the ark in 1 Samuel 4. Saul dies in battle against them on Gilboa.
early.phoenicia: Joshua and Judges place the Sidonians at Israel’s northern edge. Judges 18:7 says Laish lived quietly like them.
early.ammon: Jephthah fights Ammon in Judges 11. Nahash of Ammon besieges Jabesh Gilead, and Saul rescues it (1 Samuel 11).
early.moab: Eglon of Moab rules Israel for eighteen years until Ehud kills him (Judges 3). Ruth comes from Moab.
early.edom: Joshua 15:1 sets Judah’s southern border at Edom. Saul fights Edom in 1 Samuel 14:47.
early.midian: Midianite raiders strip Israel’s fields for seven years. Gideon drives them out in Judges 6–8.

united.israel-united: David takes Jerusalem and makes it his capital (2 Samuel 5). Solomon builds the temple there, and the kingdom splits after his death.
united.philistia: David defeats the Philistines after he becomes king (2 Samuel 5). Earlier he had lived among them at Gath and Ziklag.
united.phoenicia: Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and builders to David and Solomon. Solomon pays him in wheat and oil (1 Kings 5).
united.aram: David defeats Aram of Damascus and puts garrisons there (2 Samuel 8:5–6). Rezon later rules Damascus against Solomon (1 Kings 11:23–25).
united.ammon: Ammon shames David’s messengers, and war follows (2 Samuel 10). Joab takes Rabbah in 2 Samuel 12.
united.moab: David defeats Moab and makes it pay tribute (2 Samuel 8:2).
united.edom: David puts garrisons in Edom (2 Samuel 8:14). Hadad of Edom later troubles Solomon (1 Kings 11).
united.egypt: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter (1 Kings 3:1). Jeroboam flees to Shishak king of Egypt (1 Kings 11:40).

divided.israel-north: Kings and Chronicles follow its kings beside Judah’s. Assyria takes Samaria and deports its people in 2 Kings 17.
divided.judah: Judah keeps David’s line when the north breaks away. Its kings fight Israel, pay it, and join it by turns.
divided.aram: Ben Hadad and Hazael fight Israel for Gilead. Naaman, healed in 2 Kings 5, commands Aram’s army.
divided.phoenicia: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31). Elijah stays with a widow at Zarephath near Sidon.
divided.philistia: Philistine towns sit on Judah’s western border. Israel besieges Gibbethon, a Philistine town, twice in 1 Kings 15–16.
divided.ammon: Ammon joins Moab against Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 20. Amos 1 accuses Ammon of cruelty in Gilead.
divided.moab: Mesha king of Moab rebels after Ahab dies (2 Kings 3). A stone that Mesha set up tells his side.
divided.edom: Edom revolts against Judah in the days of Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20–22). Amos 1 accuses Edom of chasing his brother with the sword.
divided.egypt: Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple treasures from Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25–26). Hosea warns Israel against calling on Egypt.
divided.assyria-heartland: Menahem of Israel and Ahaz of Judah pay Assyria’s kings. Assyria takes Damascus, then Samaria, in 2 Kings 16–17.

late.judah: Judah stands alone after Samaria falls. Hezekiah and Josiah reform its worship while Assyria and Egypt press it.
late.assyria-empire: Sennacherib takes Judah’s walled towns and threatens Jerusalem (2 Kings 18–19). Nahum announces Nineveh’s fall.
late.egypt: Pharaoh Necoh kills Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29). He then sets Jehoiakim on Judah’s throne.
late.philistia: Hezekiah strikes the Philistines as far as Gaza (2 Kings 18:8). Zephaniah 2 warns four of their cities.
late.moab: Zephaniah 2 warns Moab for taunting Judah.
late.ammon: Zephaniah 2 warns Ammon together with Moab.
late.edom: Edom lies on Judah’s southern side in these years. The books of this period seldom name it.

babylonian.judah: Babylon takes Jerusalem and deports its people in stages. The temple burns in 2 Kings 25.
babylonian.babylon-empire: Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem and carries its people to Babylon. Jeremiah and Ezekiel speak during those years.
babylonian.egypt: Judah’s last kings look to Egypt for help against Babylon. Jeremiah is taken to Egypt after Jerusalem falls (Jeremiah 43).
babylonian.philistia: Jeremiah 47 speaks against the Philistines. Babylon’s army took their land in 604 BCE.
babylonian.phoenicia: Ezekiel 26–28 speaks against Tyre and its sea trade. Jeremiah 27 warns the kings of Tyre and Sidon to serve Babylon.
babylonian.ammon: Ammon’s king sends Ishmael to kill Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:14). Ezekiel 25 speaks against Ammon.
babylonian.moab: Jeremiah 48 speaks against Moab. Moabite raiders attack Judah in 2 Kings 24:2.
babylonian.edom: Obadiah and Lamentations 4 speak against Edom. Obadiah says Edom stood aside when strangers took Jerusalem.

persian.persia-empire: Persian kings let Judeans go home and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1; 6). Nehemiah serves the king at Susa.
persian.yehud: Zerubbabel and Jeshua rebuild the temple here. Nehemiah, as governor, rebuilds Jerusalem’s wall.
persian.samaria-province: Officials in Samaria write to the king against the builders (Ezra 4). Sanballat mocks the wall before the army of Samaria (Nehemiah 4:2).

herod.herod-kingdom: Matthew 2 sets Jesus’ birth in Herod’s days. After Herod dies, his son Archelaus rules Judea (Matthew 2:22).

gospels.judea-province: Pontius Pilate governs Judea in the Gospels (Luke 3:1). He tries Jesus in Jerusalem.
gospels.galilee-antipas: Jesus grows up and teaches in Galilee under Antipas. Antipas kills John the Baptist (Mark 6).
gospels.perea-antipas: Matthew 19:1 and Mark 10:1 take Jesus beyond the Jordan. He is on his way to Jerusalem.
gospels.philip-tetrarchy: Luke 3:1 names Philip as tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis. A tetrarch ruled one part of a divided kingdom.
gospels.decapolis: Crowds from the Decapolis follow Jesus (Matthew 4:25). The healed man of Mark 5 tells his story there.
gospels.roman-syria: Luke 2:2 dates a census by Quirinius, governor of Syria. Jesus visits the coast near Tyre and Sidon in Mark 7:24.

church.judea-province: Governors Felix and Festus hold Paul at Caesarea (Acts 23–26). Acts 12 names an earlier ruler King Herod; historians call him Agrippa I.
church.roman-syria: Believers are first called Christians at Antioch in Syria (Acts 11:26). Antioch sends out Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13.
church.cilicia: Paul comes from Tarsus in Cilicia (Acts 21:39). He passes through Syria and Cilicia in Acts 15:41.
church.cyprus: Barnabas comes from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). He and Saul cross the island from Salamis to Paphos in Acts 13.
church.galatia: Paul writes to the assemblies of Galatia. Acts 13–14 places him at Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.
church.asia: Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years (Acts 19:10). Revelation 1–3 writes to seven assemblies in Asia.
church.bithynia-pontus: The Spirit keeps Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7). First Peter greets believers in Pontus and Bithynia.
church.cappadocia: People from Cappadocia hear Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). First Peter 1:1 greets believers there.
church.macedonia: A vision calls Paul to Macedonia (Acts 16:9). He teaches in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea.
church.achaia: Paul speaks in Athens and stays in Corinth (Acts 17–18). Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, hears a charge against him.
church.crete: Paul’s ship shelters along Crete in Acts 27. Paul leaves Titus in Crete to appoint elders (Titus 1:5).
church.italy: Paul lands at Puteoli and goes on to Rome (Acts 28). Hebrews 13:24 sends greetings from the Italians.

roads.title: Via Egnatia
roads.summary: Rome built this road across Macedonia in the second century BCE. It ran from the Adriatic coast to Thessalonica and on to Byzantium.
roads.detail: Acts 16:11–17:1 takes Paul through Neapolis, Philippi, Amphipolis, Apollonia, and Thessalonica. The encyclopedia article places that trip on this road.
roads.uncertainty: Milestones mark the road as far as the edge of Thrace. The line joins known towns and smooths the bends.

roads.title: Appian Way
roads.summary: The Appian Way joined Rome with Capua and the port of Brundisium. Rome began it in 312 BCE.
roads.detail: Acts 28:15 says believers met Paul at the Market of Appius and Three Taverns. Both were stops on this road south of Rome.
roads.uncertainty: The road’s course is well known. The line joins its main towns and smooths the bends.

roads.title: Via Sebaste
roads.summary: Rome finished this army road in 6 BCE. It climbed from Perga on the coast to Antioch of Pisidia. A branch reached Iconium and Lystra.
roads.detail: Acts 13:14 takes Paul from Perga to Antioch of Pisidia. He may have used this road, but Acts does not say.
roads.uncertainty: Milestones fix parts of the road. The line between the towns is simplified.

roads.title: Cilician Gates pass
roads.summary: This pass crosses the Taurus Mountains north of Tarsus. It joins the plain of Cilicia with the high plateau.
roads.detail: Armies and traders used the pass for a very long time. Acts 15:41 sends Paul through Cilicia but does not name the pass.
roads.uncertainty: The pass is certain. The line beyond it is a broad guide.

roads.title: Persian royal road
roads.summary: Persian kings kept a road with rest stations from Sardis to Susa. Herodotus counted 111 stations on it.
roads.detail: Royal messengers changed horses at the stations. Esther 8:10 sends the king’s letters by riders on royal horses.
roads.uncertainty: Herodotus names lands and rivers, not towns. The line between Sardis and Susa is a broad guide.

road-beth-horon.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

road-lachish-jerusalem.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
road-lachish-jerusalem.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

road-kings-highway.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

road-aleppo-euphrates.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.

moses.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route mostly from Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.
moses.detailNote: The line follows Iron Age and later evidence. The books of Moses describe an earlier time.

notes.road-kings-highway: Numbers 20:17 and 21:22 name “the king’s highway” east of the Jordan.
notes.road-coastal-highway: Exodus 13:17 names a near road, “the way of the land of the Philistines.” The encyclopedia article lists that name for this coast road.

gospels.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.
gospels.detailNote: The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.

notes.road-jerusalem-jericho: Luke 10:30 sets a parable on the way down from Jerusalem to Jericho.

church.uncertainty: The sources rebuild this route from Iron Age evidence, about 1200–587 BCE. This guide has not reviewed a first-century road study for it.
church.detailNote: The line follows Iron Age evidence, not a first-century road study.

ammon.name: Ammon
ammon.summary: Ammon is the high land east of the Jordan around Rabbah.

ararat.name: Ararat
ararat.summary: Ararat is a mountain land north of Assyria.

assyria.name: Assyria
assyria.summary: Assyria is the land on the upper Tigris River.

bashan.name: Bashan
bashan.summary: Bashan is the high land east of the Sea of Galilee.

canaan.name: Canaan
canaan.summary: Canaan is the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

edom.name: Edom
edom.summary: Edom is the dry hill country south of the Dead Sea.

egypt.name: Egypt
egypt.summary: Egypt is the land along the Nile River.

galilee.name: Galilee
galilee.summary: Galilee is the hill country west of the Sea of Galilee.

lebanon.name: Lebanon
lebanon.summary: Lebanon is the mountain range north of Galilee.

midian.name: Midian
midian.summary: Midian is the land east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

moab.name: Moab
moab.summary: Moab is the high land east of the Dead Sea.

sheba.name: Sheba
sheba.summary: Sheba is a land in southern Arabia.

roadNotes.road-central-ridge: Judges 21:19 names a highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem.

details.persia-empire: Esther opens with a king who rules 127 provinces from Susa. His sealed letters reach every province.

details.judah: The poems mourn Jerusalem after its fall. Judah has gone into exile (Lamentations 1:3).
details.egypt: Lamentations 5:6 says the people gave their hand to Egypt and Assyria for bread.
details.edom: Lamentations 4:21–22 tells Edom that the cup will pass to her too.

details.babylon-empire: Daniel and his friends serve at Nebuchadnezzar’s court in Babylon.
details.judah: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and takes young nobles to Babylon (Daniel 1:1–4).

details.persia-empire: Daniel serves under Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian (Daniel 6:28).

details.babylon-empire: Daniel dates these two visions to the reign of Belshazzar king of Babylon.

details.persia-empire: Daniel dates these chapters to Darius the Mede and to Cyrus king of Persia.

details.judah: Obadiah 1:11 speaks of the day strangers entered Jerusalem’s gates and cast lots.

details.assyria-heartland: God sends Jonah to Nineveh, Assyria’s great city. Its people turn from evil, and God spares it.

details.assyria-empire: Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh, Assyria’s capital.
details.judah: Nahum 1:15 tells Judah to keep its feasts, for the enemy is cut off.
details.egypt: Nahum 3:8–10 compares Nineveh with No Amon, an Egyptian city that fell.

details.babylon-empire: God tells Habakkuk that he is raising up the Chaldeans (Habakkuk 1:6).
details.judah: Habakkuk complains of violence and unjust courts among his own people (Habakkuk 1:2–4).

details.persia-empire: Haggai dates each message by the year of Darius the king.
details.yehud: Haggai speaks to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the high priest.

details.persia-empire: Zechariah dates his first visions by the year of Darius.
details.yehud: Zechariah urges Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest to finish the temple.

details.persia-empire: Malachi 1:8 speaks of a governor over the people. The book names no king of Judah.
details.yehud: Malachi speaks to priests and people who worship at the rebuilt temple.

details.herod-kingdom: Luke 1:5 sets the story of Zacharias in the days of Herod, Judea’s king.

details.roman-syria: Luke 2:2 dates a census by Quirinius, governor of Syria.
